I will do most anything to get a good laugh.
I will make fun of my self, do insanely stupid things, and sometimes hurt myself (not in any serious way).
When I was little I didn't really understand laughter.
For some odd reason I could never tell the difference if people were laughing at something or laughing with it.
I was kind of "special" in some areas as a kid (I still am today).
Still at the tender age of five I loved making people laugh, and being special I would do even crazier things for a laugh.
Mind you I was kind of a spaz, and a really big spaz.
I was the most hyperactive five year old you will ever meet.
For example one time I hit myself in the head with a hammer, another time I was dancing around in class with a pencil in my hand, stabbed myself in the head with it, and needed stitches.
One of the craziest times though was a couple days before I had to take pictures and I wanted to go play outside, my mom knowing how "special" I was (I got it from her) wouldn't allow me to.
The expert persuasive kid I was back then convinced her to let me go outside.
Before I could even reach the street I fell head first on to the corner of the sidewalk leaving a huge mark and completely ruining the pictures.

Well I was in kindergarten and I loved school because I got to hang out with my friends and play with blocks, that might sound stupid but I was in kindergarten.
The only thing I didn't like about kindergarten was bully's.
There was this one kid in my class named Timmy.
Timmy was a bully and would pick on me all the time.
He would take my blocks, push me around, and call me names.
I didn't like Timmy at all, but I didn't know what to do about it.
One day during recess, Timmy was trying to take my ball away from me.
I was getting really upset and didn't know what to do.
I started to make funny faces at him and then I pretended to trip over my own feet.
I fell to the ground and started to roll around, pretending to be hurt.
Timmy stopped trying to take my ball and started to laugh.
He thought it was hilarious that I fell over my own feet.
All the other kids started to laugh too.
I got up and started to dance around like a monkey.
Timmy and the other kids laughed even harder.
I was so happy that I made them all laugh.
From that day on, Timmy never picked on me again.
Whenever he saw me, he would ask me to do something funny.
I didn't mind because I knew it would make him happy and he wouldn't be mean to me anymore.
After that day, I became the class clown.
I would do anything to make people laugh.
I would make funny faces, tell silly jokes, and even dance around like a monkey.
I loved making people laugh and I loved that I was able to stop Timmy from picking on me.
It can bring people together and make even the toughest situations a little bit easier.
I learned that day that laughter was the best way to deal with bullies.
Instead of fighting back or running away, I made Timmy laugh and he became my friend.
Laughter is a universal language that everyone can understand, no matter what language they speak or where they come from.
It's a way to connect with others and make the world a little bit brighter.
So if you see someone who is feeling down, try to make them laugh.
You never know, it might just change their whole day.

As dirigibles were first invented, people saw it as a new way of traveling.
After a while, they realized these blimps were really big and they weren't easy to land and refuel them.
That's when Al Smith saw it as an opportunity for his Empire State Building.
He wanted to add a mooring mast on the top of his building to allow an easier route for the dirigibles.
However, the builders faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the greatest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, rather than helium.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were also constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it difficult and unsafe for dirigibles to moor there.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
In addition, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Although two dirigibles attempted to reach the building, they were unsuccessful due to forceful winds and the lack of complete dirigible mooring equipment.
As they rebuilt it, they made the top much more complet so the Empire State Building can hold a massively heavy dirigible.
At the end of their construction the workers were very proud of themselves, but in the long run the new mooring mast didn't come to any use for multiple reasons.

One of the biggest obstacles was safety.

Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse an accident like the one that destroyed the German dirigible Hindenburg could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area like downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Finally, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
In the end, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.
A final obstacle the builders faced was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, and this made it impossible for dirigibles to dock there.
There would be no solution, even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast.
These are the obstacles the builders of the Empire State building faced in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there, in the informative excerpt, The Mooring Mast by, Marcia Amidon Lüted.

It seems as if inappropriate materials are found everywhere in today's world.
Whether it's in music, movies, or even books, there's always something that someone finds offensive.
But should these materials be removed from libraries if they are found offensive?
In my opinion, censorship in libraries is not the answer.
First of all, everyone has different opinions and beliefs.
What one person finds offensive, another person may not.
For example, one person may find a book with LGBTQ+ characters offensive, but another person may find it empowering and relatable.
If we start removing materials from libraries based on what one person finds offensive, where do we draw the line?
Soon, there would be nothing left on the shelves for anyone to read or learn from.
Secondly, libraries are meant to be a place for people to learn and explore new ideas.
By censoring materials, we limit the freedom of people to do just that.
If we only allow books that fit into a certain mold, we are not giving people the opportunity to learn about different perspectives and experiences.
This can lead to a narrow-minded society, where people are not exposed to different ideas and beliefs.
But when things are being removed because certain peolpe don't agree with them or find them offensive, that is when things are going too far.
This nation was built on the grounds of freedom for what you believe in.
So why should we force others to believe something we think?
Just because I find something offensive, doesn't mean the person next to me does, which is completely fine with me.
That is his or her own personal opinion, and what I believe should not keep him or her from learning about the things they would like to.

One way to fix this problem would be to seperate things that could possibly be found offensive into another section of the library and to put out a sign or paper saying what exactly can be found in that section.
This way, people who do not want to read or look at certain materials can avoid them, while others who are interested can still access them.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the answer.
It limits the freedom of people to learn and explore new ideas.
Instead, we should strive to create a space where everyone can access the materials they want while also respecting the values and beliefs of others.
Let's keep our libraries open and free for all to access.
As Katherine Paterson, the author, said, "if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."

As a student in junior high school, I believe that censorship in libraries is a complex issue.
On one hand, I understand that some materials may be offensive to certain individuals or groups.
However, I also believe that everyone has the right to access information and ideas, even if they may be controversial or unpopular.

Katherine Paterson, the author of many popular children's books, argues that if we start removing books that we personally find offensive, then there may be no books left on the shelf for anyone to read.
I think this is a valid point.
Everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and what one person finds offensive may not be offensive to someone else.
Therefore, it is important to have a wide range of materials available in libraries so that people can choose what they want to read based on their own interests and beliefs.
Furthermore, censorship can be a slippery slope.
If we start removing books, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what is offensive and what is not?
Should certain topics, such as sex education or LGBTQ+ issues, be censored simply because some people find them uncomfortable or disagree with them?
I think that censorship can easily lead to a suppression of ideas and a lack of diversity in thought.
However, I do believe that there should be some limitations on what is available in libraries.
For example, books that promote hate speech or violence should not be allowed.
Additionally, books that are not age-appropriate should be restricted to certain age groups.
It is important to ensure that children are not exposed to materials that could be harmful or damaging to their development.
In conclusion, I believe that censorship in libraries is a complex issue that requires careful consideration.
While some materials may be offensive to some people, everyone has the right to access information and ideas.
However, there should be some limitations on what is available in libraries to ensure that materials are age-appropriate and do not promote hate speech or violence.
At the end of the day, it is important to remember that everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and we should respect each other's right to access information and ideas.

The company doesn't go into to too much detail about what the fingerprinting involves, but it stems from a command filtering patent.
For the Super Bowl ad and other promos where Amazon already knows what's coming, Amazon will send fingerprints in advance so Alexa can compare input and ignore requests from ads.
In situations where Amazon can't predict what will happen (such as a TV segment), it uses dynamic fingerprinting that looks for many simultaneous activations based on the same audio.
This won't catch every false request, but it typically stops "80 to 90 percent" of devices from responding.
Let's put it this way -- a funny incident shouldn't devolve into national chaos.
Amazon has another technique where it can send an inaudible signal in the 3kHz to 6kHz range to stop Alexa from responding, although that doesn't appear to be in use here.

With the increasing integration of voice assistants in daily life, maintaining control over when they respond is crucial to avoid disruptions and protect user privacy.

But Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell chuckled as he mentioned the "chagrin" it would cause the Nobel committee to award Trump the world's most coveted diplomatic prize.
McConnell emphasized that while Trump's efforts in engaging with North Korea are significant, it's too early to predict the outcome or the impact it may have on global peace.
Speaking in Louisville, McConnell stated, "It's certainly premature to be discussing that," in response to questions about Trump's potential Nobel Prize candidacy.

McConnell's cautious approach reflects the sentiment that while progress is being made, there are still many uncertainties surrounding the situation.

Censorship in libraries has been a topic of debate for many years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that books should not be taken off the shelves if someone finds them offensive.
As Katherine Paterson, author of many books including "Bridge to Terabithia," said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This means that if one person has the right to remove a book they find offensive, then everyone else also has that right.
This could result in all books being removed from the shelves, leaving no books for anyone to enjoy.
Another reason why they should not be taken off the shelf is because it would be their opinion whether the book is offensive or not.
Books are meant to be read and enjoyed by everyone.
If someone takes a book off the shelf because they do not like it, this could prevent others from reading and enjoying it.
This is not fair to those who would have liked the book.
People should have the freedom to read whatever they want, and if they do not like a book, they can simply put it back on the shelf and choose another book to read.
Taking a book off the shelf because it is offensive is not the right thing to do.
It is important to respect other people's opinions and beliefs, and not force our own beliefs on others.
Additionally, taking books off the shelves because they are offensive can be harmful to the education and growth of children.
Children need to be exposed to different ideas and perspectives in order to learn and grow.
Taking books off the shelves because they are offensive can limit their exposure to different ideas and perspectives, which can hinder their education and growth.
It is important for children to learn about different cultures, religions, and beliefs, and books can play a crucial role in this.
If you do not like the book then do not read it.
But that does not mean that every one else does not like it either.
In conclusion, books should not be taken off the shelves if someone does not approve of the book.
They should be left alone to enjoy.

Patience is one of the things that people need to have.
It means that you are understanding and tolerant.
You don't get angry or upset when things don't happen as quickly as you want them to.
You wait calmly and trust that everything will work out in the end.
One time, I was waiting in line at the supermarket with my cousin and her mom.
We had a lot of items, and the line was moving slowly.
My cousin was impatient that day because she wanted to go home.
She kept on whining and complaining about how she was tired and hungry, but her mom just said, "Patience is a virtue."
Then, something happened that made my cousin realize the importance of patience.
A woman in front of us in the checkout line was having trouble counting her money.
She kept dropping coins and bills, and it was taking a long time.
My cousin was getting even more impatient, but her mom told her to be patient and wait for the woman to finish.
Finally, the woman finished counting her money and left.
When it was our turn to check out, the cashier told us that the woman had paid for our items as an apology for taking so long.
My cousin was shocked and realized that if we had been impatient and left, we would have missed out on this kind act.
From that day on, my cousin learned to be more patient.
She realized that being patient means being understanding and tolerant, even when things don't go as planned.
It also means experiencing difficulties without complaining.
Patience may not always be easy, but it can lead to unexpected rewards.

They couldn't simply drop a mooring mast on top of the building's flat roof.

The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The back of the dirigible would move from the wind, even if it was tied to the building.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Firstly, the stress of a thousand-foot dirigible held by a single cable tether would add stress to the building's frame.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.

Secondly, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Thirdly, most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another reason why it was unsafe because if some of the glass or steel part got pushed off the people down be low.
Furthermore, the law against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

The captain could not even take his hands off the control levers for fear that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.

In conclusion, the builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there, including the stress on the building's frame, shifting winds, flammability of hydrogen, safety concerns, and legal restrictions.

They argue that these materials can have a negative impact on children and can influence their behavior.

Everyone has the right to express themselves and to have access to information.
Censorship would limit this right and would prevent people from accessing information that they need or want.
It would also limit the creativity of writers and artists and would prevent them from expressing themselves freely.

Censorship in libraries is a topic that has been debated for many years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship in libraries is not necessary and that all materials should be available for people to access.
Katherine Paterson, the author of Bridge to Terabithia, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This quote perfectly captures my thoughts on censorship in libraries.
I believe that everyone has the right to read, listen to, or watch whatever they want.
Just because someone finds a piece of material offensive, it does not mean that it should be removed from the shelves for everyone else.
People have different opinions and beliefs, and it is not fair to censor materials just because a few people find them offensive.
In addition, censorship can limit people's access to important information.
For example, books about controversial topics such as racism, sexuality, and politics can educate people and help them understand different perspectives.
If these books are censored, people may not have access to the information they need to make informed decisions.
Furthermore, censorship can lead to a slippery slope.
If we start censoring materials that some people find offensive, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what is offensive and what is not?
It is a dangerous path to go down, and it can lead to an infringement on people's rights.
In conclusion, I believe that censorship in libraries is not necessary.
People have the right to access all materials, even if some find them offensive.
Censorship can limit people's access to important information and lead to a slippery slope.
It is important to remember that just because someone finds a piece of material offensive, it does not mean that it should be removed from the shelves for everyone else.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles when they attempted to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the greatest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, which is highly flammable.
The owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another obstacle was the winds on top of the building, which were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Ships were not allowed to fly too low over urban areas due to an existing law.
These all made it much harder to put a mast on the Empire State Building.

Dear editor,  I am writing to express my opinion about the effects computers have on people.
More and more people use computers, but not everyone agrees that this benefits society.
Those who support advances in technology believe that computers have a positive effect on people.
They teach hand-eye coordination, give people the ability to learn about faraway places and people, and even allow people to talk online with other people.
Some experts are concerned that people are spending too much time on their computers and less time exercising, enjoying nature, and interacting with family and friends.

They can help us to find information quickly and easily.
We can use them to talk with people from all over the world.
We can also use them to play games that challenge our minds and skills.
On the other hand, spending too much time on computers can be harmful to our health and social life.
When we are sitting in front of the computer for hours, we are not moving our bodies enough.
This can lead to health problems like obesity and back pain.
We may also become addicted to the computer and neglect our family and friends.
This can lead to loneliness and depression.
In my opinion, we should use computers in moderation.
We should use them for learning, communicating, and playing games, but we should also make time for exercise, nature, and socializing.
We should take breaks from the computer every hour or so and stretch our bodies.
We should also make time to go outside and enjoy nature.
Finally, we should spend time with our family and friends and have fun together.

Dear Editor,  As a junior high school student, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries is not the solution to offensive materials.
We should not remove books, music, movies, magazines, or any other media that we find offensive just because a few people do not like them.
If we start removing everything that offends someone, we may end up with no books or other media left on the shelves for anyone to read, listen to, or watch.
As Katherine Paterson, the author, rightly said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This means that if we start censoring materials because we find them offensive, then everyone else will also have the right to do the same.
This will ultimately lead to a situation where no one will have the opportunity to read, listen to, or watch anything that might challenge their beliefs or broaden their horizons.
If the book is thrown away no one will have the chance to read it besides the person who threw it away.
I do not believe that media that is found offensive to some of the public shouyld be removed.
Not everyone finds certain things offinsive in the media.
For example, some people might find a book about LGBTQ+ issues offensive, while others might find it informative and helpful.
Similarly, some people might find a movie about war or violence offensive, while others might find it thought-provoking and educational.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the solution to offensive materials.
Instead, we should focus on educating people about different perspectives and encouraging them to make informed choices.
We should also respect each other's right to read, listen to, or watch what we want without imposing our beliefs on others.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
All the builders had to start off by making a mooring mast at the top of the building.
They had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the building to accommodate the dirigible's load and wind pressure.
Over sixty thousand dollars worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
They designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the dirigible mast was doomed to fail because of safety concerns.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and an accident like the Hindenburg disaster could have catastrophic effects on a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas also made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

I think that there are some books out there that really do need to be taken on the library shelves and just be put in book stores for ones own useage.
Some books contain inappropriate content that can be harmful to young readers.
It is important that we protect our children from harmful material that can negatively influence their thoughts and actions.
However, we must be careful not to let censorship go too far.
Everyone has the right to read and access information, even if it may be controversial or offensive.
Censorship can limit our freedom of speech and our ability to learn from different perspectives.
As Katherine Paterson, the author of many children's books, said, "If I have the right to remove that book from the shelf...then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
If we start removing books that we find offensive, where do we draw the line?
What happens when someone else finds a book we love offensive and wants it removed as well?
Instead of censorship, we should focus on educating our children and teaching them how to think critically about the media they consume.
We should encourage them to ask questions and form their own opinions.
We should also provide resources for parents and educators to help them navigate difficult conversations with children about sensitive topics.
In conclusion, while it is important to protect our children from harmful material, censorship is not the answer.
We should strive to educate our children and promote critical thinking instead.
As Paterson said, "Without freedom of thought, there can be no such thing as wisdom - and no such thing as public liberty without freedom of speech."

However, a setback occurred last year when a federal appeals court overturned nighttime curfews and restrictions on noisy flights, emphasizing that only the FAA holds the authority to dictate flying hours.

HOUSTON — The Boston Red Sox: They’ve dropped the ball.
Boston right fielder Mookie Betts is a phenomenal defender, almost certainly the best in the game at his position.

But everyone blunders sometimes, and baseball is generally weird and postseason baseball is especially weird, and on this particular moment in the bottom of the sixth inning of Game 2 of the ALDS, Betts caught a pop-up then lost his grip on the ball while trying to make a throw.
The misplay helped extend an Astros rally that would ultimately plate four runs and extend their lead to 8-1.

To add injury to insult, Betts appeared to be in pain during his at-bat in the eighth inning, grimacing and holding his wrist after a couple of swings, and he left the game in the bottom half of the frame.
The gaffe by Betts was oddly symbolic, encapsulating the frustrations of the Red Sox in this game.
Despite his defensive prowess, even the best players can have moments of vulnerability.
The timing of the error couldn't have been worse, as it significantly impacted the course of the game and allowed the Astros to gain a significant advantage.
As Betts left the field, the concern over his potential injury only added to the disappointment felt by the Red Sox and their fans.

Censorship in libraries is a topic that has been debated for years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
Katherine Paterson, author of many children's books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This quote perfectly sums up my feelings on censorship in libraries.
The thing I read could be different from what others read.
Censorship in libraries would limit the variety of materials available to people.
It is important for people to be able to read what they want, even if it is controversial or unpopular.
For example, I personally enjoy reading books that challenge my beliefs and make me think outside of my own perspective.
If these books were censored, I would miss out on the opportunity to learn and grow as a person.
Furthermore, censorship in libraries is a violation of our First Amendment rights.
The First Amendment guarantees freedom of speech and freedom of the press.
Censorship in libraries goes against these rights by limiting what people can read and learn about.
It is important for people to be able to access information freely and make their own decisions about what they want to read and learn about.
In addition, censorship in libraries is not effective in protecting children from inappropriate materials.
If a child wants to read something that is considered inappropriate, they will find a way to do so.
It is the responsibility of parents and guardians to monitor what their children are reading and watching, not the responsibility of the library.
That why it should be a variety of things for everyone to enjoy what interest them

The Empire State Building was built as the tallest building in the World and even today still remains one of the tallest.
It had design plans with more of a purpose then just being the tallest building, however.
It was supposed to serve as a passenger exchange and a refueling dock for dirigibles.
Most people do not know this though because there were many complications involved with the architectural designs of this plan for the mast.
Architects knew it would not be easy to build such a creation and that they "could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building."
One of the main obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and if an accident were to happen above a densely populated area such as downtown New York, it would be catastrophic.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
An existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas was also a problem.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.

This digital reunion offers a unique opportunity to compare the two paintings, highlighting the subtle differences in color, composition, and brushwork that reflect Van Gogh's evolving style and emotional state.
The virtual exhibition provides an immersive experience, offering viewers a closer look at the intricate details and vibrant hues that have captivated art lovers for generations.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest problems was safety.
Most dirigibles outside of the United States used hydrogen instead of helium, which is highly flammable.

After the German dirigible Hindenburg caught fire and was destroyed in 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how dangerous it would be if an accident like that happened above a densely populated area like New York.
Another issue was the changing winds on top of the building.
Even if a dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around, making it difficult to keep it in place.
Adding weights to weigh down the back of the blimp was not practical or safe because it would be right above people walking on the streets.
Additionally, there was a law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which made it illegal for the blimp to even approach the building.
In December 1930, a U.S. Navy dirigible attempted to reach the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted to deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building, but the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, so a worker atop the mooring mast had to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The idea of using the mooring mast was eventually dropped, and by the late 1930s, dirigibles had given way to airplanes.

Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

We need to balance our screen time with other activities like sports, reading and spending time with our loved ones.

In conclusion, I believe that computers have a positive effect on people.
They help us learn, communicate and stay connected with the world.

Today, I would like to talk about censorship in libraries.
As an avid reader myself, I believe that censorship is not the answer to protecting children from potentially offensive materials.
Katherine Paterson, the author of "Bridge to Terabithia", once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
I completely agree with this statement.
If we start to remove books that we find offensive, then where does it stop?
What about movies, music, and magazines?
We would be left with nothing but a limited selection of materials.
Furthermore, censorship goes against the First Amendment of the United States Constitution, which guarantees the freedom of speech and the press.
By censoring materials, we are essentially taking away someone's right to express themselves.
It is not fair to limit someone's creativity and ideas just because we may not agree with them.
However, I do understand the concern of parents and educators who want to protect children from inappropriate content.
That is why I believe that libraries should have an age limit for certain materials.
For example, books with mature themes or explicit language should be placed in a section labeled for older readers.
Additionally, libraries can put these materials on higher shelves, making it harder for young children to access them.

Demonstrators are calling for the government to respect the independence of the judiciary and uphold the principles of democracy.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced a couple obstacles and attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Dirigibles were very long and could not exactly be held by a single cable tether.
Architects knew if the dirigible's load was placed on the building, it, ""...would add stress to the building's frame"".
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
Also, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
Docking dirigibles was a new idea for improving transportation and required builders to overcome obstacles.
The obstacles were met in the attempt to successfully allow the docking of dirigibles on the Empire state building.

Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Lastly, there was the reason of the law.
An existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

Despite the architects' efforts to modify and strengthen the building's framework and design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower with a rocket-shaped mast, the mooring mast of the Empire State Building was destined to never fulfill its purpose.
The idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.

The rooms that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world's highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.
They could've taken risks on the other theories, but on this one they had no choice.
They wouldn't be able to fight the law to allow dirigibles to fly that low.
To conclude, the obstacles faced by the builders of safety, nature, and law could not be overcome to get the mast up and working.

While attempting to allow dirigibles to dock at the Empire State building the workers faced many obstacles.
One of the obstacles was safety.
Most of the dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen instead of helium, which is highly flammable.
Therefore, if an accident like the Hindenburg disaster happened above a densely populated area like downtown New York, it could cause severe damage.
Additionally, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it impossible to dock the dirigibles.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
There are very violent winds at the top of the Empire State Building which would cause the dirigible to sway.

The obstacles that the builders were faced with in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock on the Empire State Building was that they could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.

You have to use all of your strength to swing from one bar to the next without falling.

She was swinging her legs back and forth and reaching for the next bar.

Her arms were shaking and she was having a hard time holding on.

I didn't want her to fall and hurt herself.

My sister let out the biggest fart I have ever heard in my life!

HOUSTON (AP) — A Houston 18-year-old has been arrested and charged with illegally distributing explosive-making information and attempting to support the Islamic State organization.
The U.S. Justice Department said Monday that Kaan Sercan Damlarkaya, a U.S. citizen, was arrested on Dec. 8 following an undercover FBI operation.
A statement says Damlarkaya said he intended to travel overseas and fight for IS and said he tried to get to Syria twice.

Authorities revealed that Damlarkaya had been in communication with an undercover FBI agent, expressing his desire to join the Islamic State and willingness to provide instructional materials on making explosives.
The arrest highlights the ongoing efforts to combat domestic extremism and prevent individuals from supporting terrorist organizations.
Damlarkaya faces serious charges related to his alleged involvement with IS, prompting concerns about radicalization among young individuals in the United States.
The case serves as a reminder of the importance of vigilance and swift action to prevent potential threats to national security.

Tilghman, who was shot and killed by two armed bystanders after opening fire in the restaurant, had a history of mental health issues.
The investigation into the shooting and the motive behind Tilghman's actions is ongoing.

There were many obstacles that the builders of the Empire State Building had to encounter.
Could have been the design plan or even the whole idea of building a building as large as this one could have been an obstacle in building this.
One of the major obstacles was the idea of having a mooring mast for dirigibles to dock there.

The architects had to design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
However, the greatest obstacle was the safety concern.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
That goes to show the rough conditions.
Another major obstacle that could have been was money.

The builders wanted to redo the framework which was thousands of dollars.

Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.

As Katherine Paterson, author of many award-winning children's books, said, "If I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
Censorship limits our freedom of expression and our right to access information.
It is not fair for someone to decide what is appropriate for others to read or watch.
Everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and it is important to respect that.
If we start removing books or other materials from the shelves, where do we draw the line?
Who decides what is offensive or not?
Furthermore, reading books that challenge our beliefs or make us uncomfortable can be a valuable learning experience.
It allows us to see different perspectives and learn about different cultures.
For example, reading books about the Holocaust or slavery can be difficult, but it is important to learn about these events in order to prevent them from happening again.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the solution.
It limits our freedom of expression and our right to access information.

The dirigibles were not able to dock on the mast of the Empire State Building for obvious reasons.
When the construction workers were building the mast, they didn't realize how dangerous it was having a dirigible landing on the top of the building.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Another practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.

In the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared, and the rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.

Today, I would like to share my views on censorship in libraries.
Katherine Paterson, the author of many books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
I completely agree with this statement.
Censorship is the act of removing or banning materials from public access because they are considered offensive or inappropriate.
I believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, this should only be done if the material is truly harmful and inappropriate for the intended audience.
As a junior high school student, I have seen and heard many things that are not appropriate for my age group.
I have seen students watching violent movies on their phones during class, listening to explicit music on their headphones, and even reading books with graphic content during free time.
These things can be harmful to young minds and should not be accessible to us.
However, I also believe that censorship should not be taken too far.
People should have the right to choose what they want to read, watch, or listen to.
If someone wants to read a book that may be offensive to others, they should be allowed to do so.
It is up to the individual to decide what is appropriate for them.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is a tricky subject.
While I believe that certain materials should be removed from shelves if they are found offensive, people should still have the right to choose what they want to read, watch, or listen to.
If you do not want your child to be offended or see vulgar shows, texts, and music, do not let them see it.
For instance, if a child is listening to a sexual song on their I-pod take it from them.
It is up to parents, guardians, and individuals to make responsible choices about the material they consume.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One main problem was that most dirigibles around the world used hydrogen gas which is highly flammable which can make things very dangerous at such an altitude.
The greatest obstacle to it's success was nature itself.
The winds where the docking would occur were constantly shifting and this would make the stability of the dirigible very difficult with the back end stretching so far away from the tower.
Another reason this wouldn't work was because of an already existing law against air ships flying so low over urban areas.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
The Goodyear blimp Columbia attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.

First, the frame of the Building had not been built to withstand a thousand foot long blimp docking to it.
The stress of the dirigible's weight and wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework to accommodate this new situation.

Second, the architects had to design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
Lastly, the greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In the excerpt The Mooring Mast by Marcia Amidon Lüted, the builders faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock over the Empire State Building.
The main obstacle was the safety concern as most dirigibles used hydrogen, which was highly flammable.
This was realized after the Hindenburg disaster.
Additionally, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, making it difficult to anchor the dirigibles to the mooring mast.
Even if the dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.
Furthermore, the law prohibited airships from flying too low over urban areas, which made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.

The idea of using the mooring mast was eventually shelved, and the rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden.

Going to the library you would think of it as an family environment, wouldn't you?
It's a place where you can find books, movies, and music for everyone, from children to adults.
But what happens when some people find certain materials, such as books, offensive?
Should they have the right to remove them from the shelves?
In my opinion, censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
Everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and what one person finds offensive, another person might find enlightening or even life-changing.
If we start removing books, music, and movies that some people find offensive, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what's offensive and what's not?
Katherine Paterson, author of many beloved children's books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This is a very important point.
If we start removing books that some people find offensive, we might end up removing all the books from the shelves.
Furthermore, censorship can limit our freedom of speech and expression.
If we start censoring books, music, and movies, we might start censoring other things as well, like art or political speech.
This is not what our country stands for.
We should be able to express ourselves freely, even if some people don't agree with us.
Of course, there are some materials that should not be available in libraries, like pornography or hate speech.
Most books, music, and movies are not harmful, even if some people find them offensive.
We should trust our fellow citizens to make their own decisions about what they want to read, watch, or listen to.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
It limits our freedom of speech and expression and can lead to a slippery slope where we start censoring everything.
We should trust people to make their own decisions about what they want to read, watch, or listen to, even if we don't agree with them.
As Katherine Paterson said, "We have no books left on the shelf for any of us" if we start removing books that some people find offensive.

What do you consider an offensive book?
Everyone has their own personal opinion on what they think is offensive.
But the question is, should we remove books from the shelves that are found offensive?
I say no, we should not censor books in libraries.
First of all, everyone has the right to read whatever they want.
If we start censoring books, where does it end?
Who gets to decide what is offensive and what is not?
One person's idea of offensive may not be the same as someone else's.
If we start removing books, we may end up with nothing left on the shelf.
Secondly, books are a way to learn about different cultures, ideas, and perspectives.
By reading books that we may not agree with or find offensive, we can broaden our understanding of the world around us.
We can learn about different viewpoints and experiences that we may not have been exposed to before.
By censoring books, we limit our ability to learn and grow as individuals.

It is up to parents to decide what their children can and cannot read.
If a parent does not want their child reading a certain book, they can choose not to check it out for them.
It is not up to the library to make that decision for them.
In conclusion, censorship of books in libraries is not the answer to offensive material.
Everyone has the right to read whatever they want, and books are a way to learn and grow as individuals.
We should not limit our knowledge and understanding by censoring books.
It is up to parents to decide what their children can and cannot read, not the library.
As Katherine Paterson said, "And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."

In The Mooring Mast by Marcia Amidon Lüted, it describes many ways the obstacles the builders of the Empire State Building faced in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
It was hard enough for the builders to build the Empire State Building but on top of that they must make a mooring mast at the top.
One obstacle was that the building was already extremely tall, and the mooring mast would add even more stress to the building's frame.
The stress of the dirigible's load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework to accommodate the mooring mast.
Another obstacle builders faced was having a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, only held by a single cable tether, was simply not safe.
With this being said, the steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened, costing over sixty thousand dollars worth of modifications.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.

Today, I would like to talk about censorship in libraries.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above downtown New York.
Another obstacle was the violent air currents on the top of the building.
Even if a dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast, making it unsafe for passengers to get on or off.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas was another reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building.

Despite these obstacles, the Empire State Building consulted with experts, including the U.S. Navy, and designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower with a mooring arm for docking dirigibles.
However, the idea of using the mooring mast was eventually dropped, and the rooms set aside for dirigible passengers were made over into a soda fountain and tea garden.
Dirigible were docked by means of an electric winch, which hauled in a line from the front of the ship and then tied it to a mast.
The body of the dirigible could swing in the breeze, and yet passengers could safely get on and off the dirigible by walking down a gangplank to an open observation platform.
The Empire State Building consulted with experts.
When the Empire State Building was being constructed, the main idea was to create a mooring mast for dirigibles (blimps) to dock there.
However, being the first of its kind, this idea came with many obstacles.
One of the major obstacles was the lack of a suitable landing area.
A mooring mast added to the top of the building would allow dirigibles to anchor there for several hours for refueling or service, and to let passengers off and on.
However, the stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Moreover, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
After the mast was constructed, the high speed winds were an obstacle yet again, and they wouldn't even allow dirigibles to come close to the building.
Despite how unique the idea of letting dirigibles dock on the Empire State Building was, there were many obstacles getting in the way of making the idea successful.

Hello everyone,  Have you ever been to a library or a bookstore and noticed a book that you thought was inappropriate?
Maybe it had content that was too mature or violent for your age group, or it went against your personal beliefs.
Whatever the reason, you might have wondered if it should be removed from the shelves.
This is a topic of much debate, and one that I have some strong opinions on.
As Katherine Paterson, the author of many beloved children's books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us".
I think this quote perfectly sums up my feelings on censorship in libraries.
While it might seem like a good idea to remove books that are deemed inappropriate, it sets a dangerous precedent that could lead to the removal of many more books in the future.

Everyone has different tastes and opinions, and just because something isn't to my liking doesn't mean it should be banned for everyone else.
In fact, I believe that having a wide variety of books and other materials available is essential for a healthy and diverse society.
When we start removing books because they make us uncomfortable, we are limiting our own knowledge and understanding of the world.
We are also limiting the knowledge and understanding of others who might want to read those books.
It's important to remember that just because we don't like something doesn't mean that it's not valuable or informative to someone else.
Of course, there are some situations where censorship might be necessary.
For example, if a book contains hate speech or promotes harmful behavior, it might be appropriate to remove it from the shelves.
But even in these cases, it's important to approach the situation carefully and with an open mind.
We should always strive to balance the right to free speech with the need to protect individuals from harm.
In conclusion, I believe that censorship in libraries is a complex issue that requires careful consideration.

While it's natural to want to remove materials that make us uncomfortable or go against our personal beliefs, we must be careful not to set a dangerous precedent that could lead to the removal of many more books in the future.
Instead, we should strive to promote diversity and understanding by making a wide variety of materials available to everyone.

If we start removing books and other materials that some people find offensive, where do we draw the line?

FORGET THAT OLD SAYING ABOUT NEVER taking candy from strangers.

No, a better piece of advice for the solo cyclist would be, “Never accept travel advice from a collection of old-timers who haven’t left the confines of their porches since Carter was in office.” It’s not that a group of old guys doesn’t know the terrain.
With age comes wisdom and all that, but the world is a fluid place.
At a reservoir campground outside of Lodi, California, I enjoyed the serenity of an early-summer evening and some lively conversation with these old codgers.
What I shouldn’t have done was let them have a peek at my map.
Like a foolish youth, the next morning I followed their advice and launched out at first light along a “shortcut” that was to slice away hours from my ride to Yosemite National Park.
They’d sounded so sure of themselves when pointing out landmarks and spouting off towns I would come to along this breezy jaunt.
I rode into the morning with strong legs and a smile on my face.

About forty miles into the pedal, I arrived at the first “town.” This place might have been a thriving little spot at one time—say, before the last world war—but on that morning it fit the traditional definition of a ghost town.
I chuckled, checked my water supply, and moved on.
The sun was beginning to beat down, but I barely noticed it.
The cool pines and rushing rivers of Yosemite had my name written all over them.
Twenty miles up the road, I came to a fork of sorts.
One ramshackle shed, several rusty pumps, and a corral that couldn’t hold in the lamest mule greeted me.
I had been hitting my water bottles pretty regularly, and I was traveling through the high deserts of California in June.
I got down on my hands and knees, working the handle of the rusted water pump with all my strength.
A tarlike substance oozed out, followed by brackish water feeling somewhere in the neighborhood of two hundred degrees.
I pumped that handle for several minutes, but the water wouldn’t cool down.
When I tried a drop or two, it had the flavor of battery acid.
The old guys had sworn the next town was only eighteen miles down the road.
I would conserve my water and go inward for an hour or so—a test of my inner spirit.
Not two miles into this next section of the ride, I noticed the terrain changing.
Flat road was replaced by short, rolling hills.
After I had crested the first few of these, a large highway sign jumped out at me.
It read: ROUGH ROAD AHEAD: DO NOT EXCEED POSTED SPEED LIMIT.
I was doing a water-depleting 12 mph.
Sometimes life can feel so cruel.
At some point, tumbleweeds crossed my path and a ridiculously large snake—it really did look like a diamondback—blocked the majority of the pavement in front of me.
I eased past, trying to keep my balance in my dehydrated state.
The water bottles contained only a few tantalizing sips.

Wide rings of dried sweat circled my shirt, and the growing realization that I could drop from heatstroke on a gorgeous day in June simply because I listened to some gentlemen who hadn’t been off their porch in decades, caused me to laugh.
It was a sad, hopeless laugh, mind you, but at least I still had the energy to feel sorry for myself.
There was no one in sight, not a building, car, or structure of any kind.
I began breaking the ride down into distances I could see on the horizon, telling myself that if I could make it that far, I’d be fi ne.
Over one long, crippling hill, a building came into view.
I wiped the sweat from my eyes to make sure it wasn’t a mirage, and tried not to get too excited.
With what I believed was my last burst of energy, I maneuvered down the hill.
In an ironic twist that should please all sadists reading this, the building—abandoned years earlier, by the looks of it—had been a Welch’s Grape Juice factory and bottling plant.
A sandblasted picture of a young boy pouring a refreshing glass of juice into his mouth could still be seen.
That smoky blues tune “Summertime” rattled around in the dry honeycombs of my deteriorating brain.
I got back on the bike, but not before I gathered up a few pebbles and stuck them in my mouth.
I’d read once that sucking on stones helps take your mind off thirst by allowing what spit you have left to circulate.
With any luck I’d hit a bump and lodge one in my throat.
I was going to die and the birds would pick me clean, leaving only some expensive outdoor gear and a diary with the last entry in praise of old men, their wisdom, and their keen sense of direction.
I made a mental note to change that paragraph if it looked like I was going to lose consciousness for the last time.
Somehow, I climbed away from the abandoned factory of juices and dreams, slowly gaining elevation while losing hope.
Then, as easily as rounding a bend, my troubles, thirst, and fear were all behind me.
GARY AND WILBER’S FISH CAMP—IF YOU WANT BAIT FOR THE BIG ONES, WE’RE YOUR BEST BET!
“And the only bet,” I remember thinking.

As I stumbled into a rather modern bathroom and drank deeply from the sink, I had an overwhelming urge to seek out Gary and Wilber, kiss them, and buy some bait—any bait, even though I didn’t own a rod or reel.
An old guy sitting in a chair under some shade nodded in my direction.
Cool water dripped from my head as I slumped against the wall beside him.
“Where you headed in such a hurry?” “Yosemite,” I whispered.
“Know the best way to get there?” I watched him from the corner of my eye for a long moment.
He was even older than the group I’d listened to in Lodi.
I own a very good map.” And I promised myself right then that I’d always stick to it in the future.
