Builders of the Empire State Building faced many challenges while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of them was not being able to just drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building's flat roof.
This was because a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The architects could not build a utilitarian mast without any ornamentation.
They designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
The other obstacles included safety concerns as most dirigibles used hydrogen rather than helium, which is highly flammable.
Also, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Lastly, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In a proactive effort to protect the endangered Puget Sound orcas, lawmakers have introduced a series of bills aimed at addressing the various threats facing these iconic marine mammals.
The proposed legislation tackles key issues such as vessel noise and disturbance, pollution, and declining prey availability, all of which have contributed to the decline of the orca population.
One of the key components of the bills is a focus on reducing vessel traffic in orca habitats, as noise from boats can disrupt the whales' ability to communicate and hunt for food.
Additionally, measures to reduce pollution in the waters of Puget Sound are being considered to improve the overall health of the orcas and their ecosystem.
Furthermore, efforts to enhance salmon habitat and increase salmon hatchery production are also part of the proposed legislation, as salmon are a vital food source for the orcas.
By addressing these critical issues, lawmakers hope to reverse the decline of the Puget Sound orcas and ensure their long-term survival in the region.
Jay Inslee’s supplemental budget also devotes $3 million to help the whales by increasing vessel enforcement, improving salmon habitat and increasing salmon hatchery production.

For some people, a local library can be where they spend most of their time.
Everyone remembers going to the library as a child, and picking out your favorite book to read.
The wide variety of different subjects or stories found in these books are practically endless.
There is one question, however, that many people wonder about the library.
Are some of the materials- such as books, magazines, movies- too offensive to some people?
I believe the offensive material in libraries should not be removed, however, it should be isolated to one particular spot, so everyone can know which area contains the material.
There are many reasons I believe this.
One reason is that I believe that some materials are not ment for children and some young adults to see.
The least a library could do is keep one section for just the children, and another section for the potentially offensive materials.
However, the responsiblity of keeping the children from wandering near the offensive material should be in the hands of the parent.

Another reason that the offensive materials should be one held in a particular section of the library, is that sometimes young adults, or even adults, can unknowingly pick up a book that contains offensive material.
I'm sure that nearly all of us have been in a situation in which we started reading a book, and the story ended up to be something completely different from what we expected.
However, some people might argue that the offensive materials should be removed from the library because it is not appropriate for some people to read or see.
But, I believe that everyone has the right to read or see whatever they want.
We should not limit the materials available in the library because it might offend someone.
It is important to remember that everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and what is offensive to one person might not be offensive to another.
One reason I believe the material should not be completely removed from the library is illustrated in the shown quote by author Katherine Paterson.
If a person could just remove a book from the library because they thought it was offensive, then more and more people would start doing this.
Then, before we know it, there would be no more books left to check out.
All in all, I do not believe that the offensive material should be removed from the library.
I do believe, however, that the offensive material should be kept in one section of the library, so that no one accidentally picks up a book/magazine that contains offensive material.

Limited access and restrictions on the types of businesses allowed to purchase goods from the market highlight the complexities of Cuba's economic transition.
The success of this initiative will depend on how effectively it addresses the needs of private enterprises and contributes to a more diverse and competitive business environment.

The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.

Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

I'm here to talk about censorship in libraries.
Do you believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive?
As a junior high school student, I believe that censorship is not the answer.
First of all, everyone has different opinions and beliefs.
What may be offensive to one person may not be offensive to another.
For example, some people may find a book containing LGBTQ+ themes offensive, while others may find it informative and necessary for representation.
Who gets to decide what is offensive and what is not?
Should one person or group have the power to dictate what everyone can or cannot read, watch, or listen to?
Moreover, censorship can limit access to important information and ideas.
For instance, historical books about wars or social justice movements may contain graphic descriptions or language, but they also provide valuable insights and lessons.
By censoring these materials, we are depriving ourselves and future generations of knowledge and understanding.
Furthermore, censorship can lead to a slippery slope.
If we allow certain materials to be removed because they are deemed offensive, where do we draw the line?
What happens when someone else finds a different book or song offensive?
Will we continue to remove materials until there is nothing left on the shelves?
In addition, parents and guardians have the responsibility to monitor what their children read, watch, or listen to.

Libraries already have systems in place, such as age restrictions and parental consent, to ensure that children do not have access to materials that are not appropriate for their age or maturity level.
It is not the responsibility of the library to censor materials for the entire community.
Lastly, censorship goes against the First Amendment, which guarantees freedom of speech and expression.
By censoring materials, we are limiting this fundamental right and infringing on the rights of individuals to make their own choices.
In conclusion, censorship is not the answer.
It limits access to important information and ideas, can lead to a slippery slope, and goes against our fundamental rights.
Let's trust individuals to make their own choices and allow everyone to have access to a variety of materials.

TAYLORSVILLE, N.C. (AP) — Where do you hide a 1,000-pound chicken?
That's what sheriff's deputies in Alexander County, North Carolina, are trying to figure out as they search for the concrete statue that disappeared from a farm west of Taylorsville over the weekend.
While the chicken may be heavy, it's only 3 feet tall.
Deputies think the statue was taken sometime between 8 p.m. Saturday and 9 a.m. Sunday from the driveway of the farm.
Chief Deputy Tod Jones told the Hickory Daily Record (http://bit.ly/2l7Z6BF) the statue's base was found several miles away.
The missing concrete bird has left the farm owners and local community puzzled and concerned.
The unique half-ton statue had become a beloved landmark in the area, attracting visitors and becoming a symbol of the farm's identity.
Authorities are urging anyone with information about the missing chicken to come forward and help solve the mystery of its disappearance.
Meanwhile, the farm owners are hopeful for the safe return of their prized concrete bird.

The Senate has given the green light to a groundbreaking measure that could potentially revolutionize epilepsy treatment.
The bill, which allows for the use of oil derived from the cannabis plant to treat epilepsy, marks a significant step forward in the field of medical cannabis.
Indiana, known for its strict stance on marijuana-related issues, is among the last states to consider such a measure.

The proposed legislation aims to address intractable epilepsy by permitting the use of cannabidiol, or CBD, a non-psychoactive compound found in cannabis that has shown promise in reducing epileptic seizures.
The bill establishes a registry for qualified physicians, nurses, individuals, and caregivers to administer CBD treatment and authorizes pharmacies to dispense the oil.
The Senate has now passed the bill to the House for further review and potential approval.

An important amendment to the legislation replaced mentions of "hemp oil" with cannabidiol, defining it as an extract containing less than 0.3 percent THC, at least 5 percent CBD, and no other controlled substances.

Indiana is among the last states to forbid even the issue of marijuana extracts that are low in THC and high in cannabidiol, or CBD, the compound that studies suggest may help reduce epileptic seizures.
The measure creates a registry for some physicians, nurses, individuals and caregivers to treat intractable epilepsy with cannabidiol and permits pharmacies to dispense it.
The Senate has sent it to the House for consideration.
An amendment to the bill replaced references to “hemp oil” with cannabidiol.
The measure defines cannabidiol as a plant extract or mixture containing less than 0.3 percent THC, at least 5 percent CBD and no other controlled substance.
